01

The bill already exists. Nobody added it up.

To spend less you first have to know where it went — and that record is already sitting on your disk. Every session writes one.

Nothing to install, nothing to switch on. The hub reads 154 sessions and $4,348 at list prices straight out of the files Claude Code already keeps. Each row shows how much text that session carried and a first guess at what it could have cost instead.

02

Five sessions are 80% of the bill.

This one fact tells you where to look, and it takes a single click on the Cost column.

$1,254 + $964 + $531 + $377 + $356 = $3,482 of the $4,348. Spend your time anywhere else and you are polishing the small stuff.

03

What you could save — and how much of that is a guess.

This is the saving potential: a number per session, with its own confidence attached. A figure you cannot question is no use.

$617 to $1,234 of $1,253.85. priced means we took this session’s own text and re-priced it at another model’s published rate — real arithmetic, but a best case nobody actually reaches. guess means a range with a reason and no proof. detector means we measured, and the answer is no.

The last one earns its place here. 97% of the text was already being reused from the cache, so there is nothing left for caching to save. Anyone offering you a caching win on this session is measuring something else.

04

Most of the money went on re-sending the conversation.

Which saving is worth chasing depends on where the money actually goes. A single total hides this completely.

Re-sent text cost $817, which is 65% of the bill, even though it is charged at a tenth of the normal rate. Brand new text cost four cents. The conversation grew until each request was carrying 779,000 tokens, and stayed there.

05

Pick a strategy to try.

A saving potential is still an opinion. Choosing a strategy is how it becomes a measurement — a cheaper model, a shorter conversation, a different cache setting.

★ marks the strategies this session’s own numbers point at. Auto lets a model pick when you do not know yet. Whichever you choose, the original setup is run again alongside it, so there is something honest to compare against.

06

Sixty-seven cents to settle it.

The reason to test rather than argue is that testing is cheap and arguing is not.

Three runs, each in its own cloud sandbox, using this session’s real files and its real request. About two minutes. The hub had already warned that this session was too small to be worth measuring — it only cost $0.22 in the first place. We ran it anyway, to show the whole loop.

07

The report, in one picture.

Six things you care about on six spokes, one outline per run. Further from the centre is better, so the shape of an outline is the trade it made.

The cheap run reaches the rim on cost and collapses towards the centre on nearly everything else — lowest score, ten turns instead of five, and no cache reuse at all. The original and the no-change run trace almost the same shape, which is the first hint that the second one did not really change anything.

baseline — the original setup
exp1 — the cheap model
exp2 — the run that changed nothing

The chart keeps the short names the run used: baseline is the original setup, exp1 the cheap model, exp2 the one meant to turn off compaction. Every spoke prints its three values, so no shape has to be taken on trust.

08

Cheaper and worse, with the number attached.

Both halves matter. “Cheaper” on its own is the result that gets rolled out and then regretted.

7.1 times cheaper, and 18 points worse out of 60. The scorer said what was actually wrong rather than just marking it down: the cheap model accepted True as if it were the number 1, so asking for the Roman numeral of True gave back "I" instead of an error. It also left a stray build file next to its tests. No price table can see that.

09

And it says when a run proved nothing.

The report opens by stating what each run actually changed, worked out by comparing the settings rather than trusting the label someone typed. That caught a real problem here.

Something you can show to someone who disagrees — and it is the same report the command line produces for a benchmark.

One of the three runs changed nothing at all. The planner asked for “no compaction” on a setup that already had compaction off. Its 37% price gap and 3-point score gap are simply two goes at the same thing — normal variation, not a finding. Without that check it would have been written up as a win.

One pass answers one question. The cheap model is not safe on this kind of work at this standard. That will not stay true forever — a different job, a different spec, a new model release, and it is worth asking again. Every session you finish is a new candidate, and at 67 cents a go, asking again is routine rather than a project.
